results.title: Cross compilation - pypackaging-native
results.content: The way build backend hooks in `pyproject.toml` are specified (see PEP 517) means cross-platform compilation support has been partially converted into a concern for individual build systems to manage. In order to cross-compile a Python package, one needs a compiler toolchain as well as two Python installs - one for the build system and one for the host system.1 This can make it a little challenging to get started. More general-purpose packaging ecosystems often have toolchains and supporting infrastructure to cross-compile packages for their own needs - see, e.g., info for Void Linux, conda-forge, Debian and Nix. Tools like crossenv can be used to trick Python into performing cross-platform builds. While a build system like Meson or CMake may support cross-platform compilation, and a project may be able to cross-compile binary artefacts, invocation of a `pyproject.toml` build hook typically assumes that the platform running the build will be the platform that ultimately runs the Python code.

Manual testing is required to ensure a cross-platform app’s performance and functionality across multiple devices and platforms. Regarding expenses, native apps cost more because they need separate codebases for each platform, while hybrid applications reduce development costs by allowing code sharing.
